summary: Discusses design goals for a network-based localized mobility management protocol, in which the network rather than the host handles movement within a local domain. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a device moves around a building, the network could track and follow it. This lists what such a system should achieve before anyone designs it.

questions: when do you need localized mobility management
subtitle: Design goals for having the network track mobile devices instead of requiring software updates on phones.

tldr.problem: Mobile devices moving between wireless access points need IP address changes, causing dropped connections and requiring complex software on phones. Global mobility protocols like Mobile IPv6 work everywhere but are overkill for moving within a building. Proprietary wireless switch approaches work well but are not interoperable.
tldr.mechanism: Network-based localized mobility management (NETLMM) lets the network infrastructure handle device movement within a local area. A local mobility anchor maintains routes for each device, and edge access gateways update those routes when devices move. The phone needs no special mobility software for local movement.
tldr.outcome: Devices can move around a building or campus without dropping connections or changing IP addresses, with faster handovers and less signaling than host-based protocols, while remaining interoperable across vendors.

facts.label: Signaling reduction
facts.value: From 18 messages (Mobile IPv6) to only movement detection signaling

facts.label: IP address behavior
facts.value: Device keeps same address while moving within local domain

today: RFC 4831 is an Informational RFC defining design goals for network-based localized mobility management. It led to the development of the Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) protocol, which implements these goals and is deployed in cellular networks and enterprise WiFi systems.

sections.title: The Mobility Problem
sections.content:
Mobile devices face a fundamental problem: the Internet is built on the assumption that a device's IP address indicates both its identity and its location. When a device moves from one wireless access point to another, it moves to a new IP subnet and needs a new IP address. This causes running connections to break.

Global mobility protocols like Mobile IPv6 solve this by letting a device keep one permanent home address and tunnel traffic through a home agent, but they add complexity and overhead everywhere, even for short local movements. Proprietary WLAN switch solutions work well within one vendor's equipment but are not interoperable. The goal is a network-based solution that works like the WLAN switches but with open standards and no special software required on phones.
sections.plainLanguage: IP addresses are like mailbox numbers that say both who you are and where you are. When you move, you need a new mailbox number, so your mail does not reach you. We need a system where the network knows where you are and redirects your mail automatically, without you having to do anything special.

sections.title: How NETLMM Works
sections.content:
The NETLMM architecture has two main components. A Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) is a router in the backbone network that maintains a routing table with one entry for each mobile device in the local mobility domain. It tracks which access point each device is connected to. A Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) is the access point itself (or a router controlling it), and it communicates with the LMA using NETLMM signaling.

When a mobile device moves from one access point to another, the new MAG detects the movement and sends a route update to the LMA. The LMA updates its table to point to the new MAG. From that point on, packets destined for the mobile device are tunneled from the LMA to the new MAG, which forwards them to the device. The device can keep the same IP address throughout its movement within the local domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the LMA as a post office that knows where everyone lives. The MAGs are local mail carriers. When you move to a new apartment (access point), the local mail carrier tells the post office, and mail gets rerouted. You keep the same address the whole time.

sections.title: Key Design Goals
sections.content:
The RFC lists eleven goals for NETLMM. The first three address the core problems: Goal 1 is to reduce handover latency below 70 milliseconds so real-time calls like voice remain uninterrupted. Goal 2 is to minimize signaling from the mobile node, reducing the number of control messages from roughly 18 (as required by Mobile IPv6) down to just what is needed for movement detection. Goal 3 is to preserve location privacy by allowing a device to keep the same IP address despite moving to different locations.

Goal 4 limits overhead in the access network, since wireless links have limited capacity. Goal 5 simplifies security by deriving it from network access authentication rather than requiring new security associations. Goal 6 makes the protocol work with any wireless link type without vendor-specific knowledge. Goal 7 supports unmodified mobile nodes – no special software needed on phones. Goals 8, 9, and 10 ensure the protocol works for both IPv4 and IPv6, reuses existing protocols where sensible, and operates independently of global mobility protocols.

Goal 11 allows operators to choose their preferred forwarding method between the LMA and MAGs, such as IP tunneling or IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: Fast handovers, less signaling, keep your address hidden, works with all wireless types, needs no phone software, compatible with IPv4 and IPv6, reuses existing protocols, and lets operators choose how data travels between the access network and backbone.

sections.title: Why NETLMM Instead of Alternatives
sections.content:
Host-based global mobility protocols like Mobile IPv6 put complexity on the phone: the phone must detect movement, reconfigure its address, authenticate to mobility services, and maintain bindings with home agents and correspondent nodes. This consumes battery, requires frequent software updates to phones, and makes it hard to support multiple mobility protocols.

Proprietary WLAN switches work well from an operational perspective – they require no phone changes – but they are tied to one vendor, only work for one wireless technology, and lack interoperability. NETLMM aims for the best of both: the operational convenience of WLAN switches with the openness and interoperability of IETF standards. By having the network detect movement through link-layer or IP-layer signaling and manage mobility centrally, phones can remain unmodified and work with any global mobility protocol or none at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Global protocols like Mobile IPv6 make phones work hard and drain batteries. Proprietary WLAN switches are convenient but lock you into one vendor. NETLMM gives you the convenience without the lock-in, and without draining your phone's battery.

sections.title: Security in NETLMM
sections.content:
NETLMM faces two kinds of security challenges. First, security between a mobile node and the network: the MAG must securely identify the mobile node and confirm it is authorized to move. This can be achieved through existing network access authentication mechanisms like 802.1x or through IP-layer security like SEND (Secure Neighbor Discovery).

Second, security between network elements: the communication between the MAG and LMA must be protected from attack and unauthorized route updates. The RFC does not specify how this is done but notes that it should derive from existing security infrastructure rather than requiring new associations.

Detailed threat analysis and specific security mechanisms are covered in separate IETF documents referenced by this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The network must know for certain that a phone is who it claims to be when it moves. The connection between network elements must be secure so attackers cannot trick the network into rerouting traffic. The goal is to use existing security tools rather than inventing new ones.
